newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 25.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LONDON HOUSE PRICES UP 21 PERCENT

According to the Nationwide Building Society, the difference in house prices between the north and the south of Britain is continuing to widen. London prices are 21 percent higher than a year ago, but northern prices are still depressed. Nationwide's findings are in line with those from the Halifax. Nationwide's head of research, Paul Sanderson, said that prices were booming because there is a shortage of homes for sale.
-- J ROTHSCHILD MD QUITS JUST TWO WEEKS AFTER TAKEOVER

Keith Carby has resigned as managing director of J Rothschild Assurance, the life assurer, with 11 million stg. He refuses to say why he made the decision. Two weeks ago, St James's Place Capital, a financial services company bought the 56 percent of J Rothschild it did not already own, valuing the group at 379 million stg. Carby says he created the whole thing from scratch, designing the sales and marketing.
-- MCI PROFITS FLAT AS IT PREDICTS SLOWER GROWTH

MCI Communications, the U.S. long-distance telephone company being bought by British Telecom for $23 billion, reported flat net profits of $295 million after competition and investment in new markets held back earnings. BT's takeover promises to benefit MCI's executives and managers, with a $100 million bonus pool being set up to help retain key employees.
THE TIMES
-- REGAN ENDS BID AS NOMURA PULLS OUT

Japanese bank Nomura has pulled its 1.2-billion-stg support for a bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society by Andrew Regan and David Lyons. CWS reacted by starting criminal proceedings against the two and Allan Green, the CWS executive who admits he gave Regan and Lyons confidential material. The collapse of the bid should clear the way for Lanica's shares to be re-listed in the next few days.
-- BARCLAYS BREAKS RANKS WITH BANKS ON MONETARY UNION

Barclays Bank has warned customers that it is not preparing to have euro retail banking services ready for early monetary union, unlike other banks who say they would offer euro accounts from the start of the single currency. Barclays does not want to waste money, anticipating sterling will not join the euro in the first wave. It stands against recommendations from the Bank of England that suggest banks should go ahead so they can start euro operations if needed.
-- TUNNEL'S REFINANCE PROPOSALS ATTACKED

Richard Hannah, transport secretary at UBS Securities has warned that Eurotunnel's 2.2-billion-stg refinancing plans do not go far enough. The proposals would cut Eurotunnel's 8.7-billion-stg debt by 1.1 billion stg immediately and by another 1.1 billion stg in six years. The plans have been agreed by the steering group of six banks but will not go before the 225-strong banking syndicate until October. Three shareholding groups in France are planning to block the proposals.
THE GUARDIAN
-- COAL FIRM SEEKS GAS DEAL CURBS

Coal producers in the UK are demanding that European competition authorities investigate alleged "sweetheart" deals and predatory pricing by gas-fired electricity generators. They claimed such practices could force all coal-fired generators out of the mainstream electricity market by next year. This development will reopen the controversy surrounding the race to build gas-fired stations.
-- GLAXO GIVES UP ZANTAC BATTLE

Glaxo has called off a three-year, multi-million-stg battle in the US Supreme Court to defend Zantac, the drug on which the pharmaceutical company built its fortune, after losing a court case against NovoPharm, a Canadian generic drugs maker that won permission to market a rival drug. Glaxo is resigned to rivals moving in and has signalled that its revenues from the product might halve within two years.
-- STRONG POUND SQUEEZES PROFITS

The Office for National Statistics says the pound's rise on the foreign exchange is denting British exports and squeezing manufacturing profits. ONS reported a deepening trade deficit, with a shortfall of 758 million stg in February. ICI and Vickers, two of Britain's top manufacturing companies, blamed the pound for the squeeze in their margins. A strong pound makes exports more expensive. City analysts said the figures backed the firms' claim of a loss of competitiveness.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- LAURA ASHLEY RECOVERY STALLS

The chief executive of Laura Ashley, Ann Iverson, admitted her recovery programme for the fashion and fabrics group had run into trouble this year, leading to a collapse in shares. A year ago share were trading double the current level. She said delays in store openings meant her sales targets for garment ranges were not being met and the company would have to cut prices to shift unsold merchandise.
-- INVESCO FINED BY IMRO FOR THE THIRD TIME

Imro has announced it fined Invesco 60,000 stg for breaching its rules on handling client money, following two other fines in 1993 and 1991. Breaches include failing to reconcile client money bank accounts on time, failing to correct differences on reconciliations, and failing to maintain written compliance procedures. Imro said Invesco had accepted it had failed on a number of occasions to reconcile its own records of client account balances with the bank in which these funds were kept.
-- GOVERNMENT URGED TO COOL ECONOMY BY RAISING TAXES

The British Chambers of Commerce says the next government should raise taxes rather than interest rates to cool the overheating economy. It warned of wage pressures at home because of skill shortages and damage to sales overseas because of the strong pound. This is backed by a new forecast from the London Business School that predicts growth will exceed three percent this year.
